newsitem.title: USA: U.S. jobless rate rose to 5.2 percent in September.
newsitem.headline: U.S. jobless rate rose to 5.2 percent in September.

text.p: The unemployment rate rose to 5.2 percent last month from 5.1 percent in August as the number of jobs in the economy shrank for the first time since January, the Labour Department said Friday.

In the government's first assessment of the economy's health in September, the department said the number of non-farm jobs declined by a seasonally adjusted 40,000 during the month after payrolls grew by a solid 241,000 in August.
Wall Street economists surveyed by Reuters had projected a September unemployment rate of 5.2 percent and the creation of 166,000 jobs.

Economic data have been erratic, but most recently have pointed to slower activity in the manufacturing sector. Federal Reserve policymakers decided last week to leave interest rates unchanged, at least until their next meeting in mid-November, giving encouragement to financial markets.
The bond market rallied, and is expected to give stocks a boost, as the data eased worries about inflation, reinforcing hopes that the Fed will not raise interest rates soon.
Shortly after 9 a.m. EDT, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was up 26/32, lowering the yield to 6.77 percent from 6.84 percent at Thursday's close.

"It's very clear the economy slowed in September. It's obviously very good news for the Federal Reserve and for the bond market but a mixed blessing for stocks because it will intensify worries about earnings," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany.

Workers' average hourly earnings, which have been closely watched recently for signs of wage-push pressure on prices, rose by 6 cents last month to $11.92 after rising 5 cents in August. Over the past year, earnings rose 3.5 percent.

Last month's job drop, the first since a decline of 66,000 jobs in January, was paced by a drop in factory jobs and public school employment, which was affected by statistical factors, the department said. Over the past year job growth has averaged nearly 200,000 a month.

In the slowing industrial sector, manufacturing employment fell by a hefty 57,000 in September after gaining 18,000 in August, the department said. Since March 1995, the number of factory jobs has shrunk by 331,000, it said.
The factory work week rose by 6 minutes last month to 41.8 hours, while overtime was unchanged at 4.5 hours a week.
Employment in service-producing industries, usually quite strong, grew only by a mere 10,000 last month after expanding by 211,000 in August.

A key factor was an 81,000-job drop in government employment in September. This included a decline of 67,000 local teaching jobs that the department blamed on the impact of changing school years on its method of adjusting data for seasonal factors. In August, the number of local teaching jobs rose by 85,000.

"Due to changes in school schedules, there were larger returns to payrolls prior to September this year than were expected by our seasonal factors," said Katharine Abraham, commissioner of the department's Bureau of Labour Statistics.
"This accounts for the large increases, on a seasonally adjusted basis, in local education employment over the summer and for this month's sharp decline," she said in a statement.

The department's survey of households showed that the number of jobless workers rose by 141,000 last month to 6.97 million, while those with jobs rose by 313,000 to 127.37 million, the depatment said. The civilian labour force, which includes employed workers and those seeking jobs, grew by 455,000 to 134.34 million, it said.
